sections.heading: Meaning and scope of biology
paragraphs: Biology is the scientific study of life and living organisms. The word comes from the Greek bios (life) and logos (study). It spans the molecular processes inside cells, the structure and behavior of organisms, interactions among species, and the functioning of ecosystems.

The subject includes basic sciences such as botany, zoology, microbiology, genetics, cell biology, physiology and ecology, as well as applied fields such as medicine, agriculture, biotechnology and environmental science. These fields overlap because living systems operate across many levels, from molecules and cells to organisms and populations.

sections.heading: Shared characteristics of living things
bullets: Cellular organization: all organisms consist of one or more cells, the basic units of life.
Metabolism: organisms obtain and transform matter and energy through chemical reactions, including building reactions (anabolism) and breakdown reactions (catabolism).
Homeostasis: organisms regulate internal conditions, such as temperature, water balance or pH, despite external change.
Growth and development: organisms increase in size or cell number and undergo orderly changes during their life cycles.
Response to stimuli: organisms detect and respond to changes in their surroundings.
Reproduction and heredity: organisms produce offspring and pass genetic information to them; populations can evolve across generations.
Adaptation: inherited characteristics that improve survival or reproduction can become more common in a population over time.

sections.heading: Origin of life: major historical explanations
bullets: Special creation explains life as the result of creation by a divine power; it is a religious explanation rather than an experimentally testable scientific hypothesis.

Spontaneous generation proposed that life could arise directly from nonliving matter under ordinary conditions. Experiments by Redi and later Pasteur challenged this claim and supported biogenesis: living organisms arise from pre-existing life under observed conditions.

Catastrophism proposed repeated creations following large catastrophes. Panspermia proposed that life or its precursors arrived from space, but it does not explain the original origin of life and lacks decisive evidence.

Chemical evolution proposes that simple chemicals on early Earth formed increasingly complex molecules and eventually systems capable of replication and evolution. It is a scientific research framework; details of the earliest steps remain under investigation.
Do not confuse the origin of the first life with biological evolution: evolution explains how populations change and diversify after life exists.

sections.heading: Scientific method and experimental reasoning
bullets: A typical investigation begins with observation and a focused question, followed by a testable hypothesis and a prediction derived from it.
Researchers design a fair test, define variables, collect and analyze evidence, then decide whether results support, refute or require revision of the hypothesis.

The independent variable is deliberately changed; the dependent variable is measured. Controlled variables are kept as consistent as practical. A control group provides a comparison without the experimental treatment.
A scientific theory is a broad, evidence-supported explanation that unifies many observations. It is not simply a guess. A hypothesis is a narrower testable proposal.
Repeatable methods, careful measurement, sufficient sample size, honest reporting and peer scrutiny make conclusions more reliable. Correlation alone does not prove cause and effect.

sections.heading: Exam review
bullets: Define biology and give examples of both basic and applied branches.
Explain how metabolism, homeostasis and response to stimuli differ.
Compare chemical evolution with spontaneous generation and distinguish origin of life from evolution.
Identify independent, dependent and controlled variables in a simple experiment.

topics.title: 2.1 Organic and inorganic molecules of life

sections.heading: Water, minerals and chemical bonds
bullets: Water is polar and forms hydrogen bonds. Its solvent properties allow many reactions and transport processes; its high specific heat moderates temperature change, and cohesion helps produce surface tension.
Mineral ions support functions such as nerve signaling, bone structure, enzyme activity and osmotic balance. Their required amounts vary by organism and ion.

Covalent bonds share electrons and hold atoms together within molecules. Ionic interactions involve charged particles; hydrogen bonds are weaker attractions important in water and in the structure of large biomolecules.
Condensation (dehydration synthesis) joins smaller subunits and releases water; hydrolysis uses water to break bonds. These processes build and digest biological polymers.

sections.heading: Carbohydrates
paragraphs: Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen and include sugars and polysaccharides. Monosaccharides such as glucose are single sugar units; disaccharides contain two linked sugars; polysaccharides are long chains.
bullets: Glucose is an important cellular fuel. Sucrose, lactose and maltose are familiar disaccharides with different component sugars.
Starch stores glucose in plants; glycogen stores it in animals and fungi. Cellulose forms strong plant cell walls and is not digested by human enzymes.
Carbohydrates can supply energy, store energy, provide structural support and participate in cell recognition.

sections.heading: Lipids
paragraphs: Lipids are a diverse group that includes triglycerides, phospholipids, waxes and steroids. Many are hydrophobic and do not dissolve readily in water.
bullets: A triglyceride consists of glycerol joined to three fatty acids. Fats are generally solid and oils liquid at room temperature; both store energy and provide insulation and cushioning.
Saturated fatty acids have no carbon-carbon double bonds; unsaturated fatty acids have one or more. Their shapes affect packing and physical state.
Phospholipids have water-attracting heads and water-avoiding tails, so they form the basic bilayer of cell membranes.
Steroids include cholesterol, a membrane component and precursor for some signaling molecules. Waxes provide water-resistant coatings.

sections.heading: Proteins
paragraphs: Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. The sequence of amino acids determines how the chain folds, and its three-dimensional shape strongly affects its function.
bullets: Proteins function as enzymes, structural materials, transporters, receptors, antibodies, contractile elements and signaling molecules.
Enzymes lower activation energy and speed specific reactions without being used up. Their active sites bind substrates; temperature, pH, substrate concentration and inhibitors can affect activity.
Changes in conditions can denature a protein by disrupting its shape. A denatured enzyme may no longer bind its substrate effectively.
Amino acids differ in their side chains. A protein's primary sequence influences higher levels of structure and ultimately its biological role.

sections.heading: Nucleic acids and ATP
bullets: DNA and RNA are nucleic acids made from nucleotide subunits. Each nucleotide contains a sugar, phosphate and nitrogenous base.

DNA stores hereditary information, usually as a double helix with complementary base pairs A-T and C-G. RNA uses uracil (U) instead of thymine (T) and participates in gene expression and protein synthesis.
ATP is a nucleotide that transfers usable energy to cellular processes when its terminal phosphate is transferred or removed. It is continually regenerated by metabolism.
A balanced exam comparison should state each molecule's building block, major structure and main function rather than saying only that all are important.

sections.heading: Exam review
bullets: Compare starch, glycogen and cellulose by organism, role and digestibility.
Explain how phospholipid structure allows a bilayer to form in water.
Trace how amino-acid sequence relates to protein shape and enzyme function.
Describe the components of a nucleotide and distinguish DNA from RNA.

units.title: Chapter 3 - The Cellular Basis of Life

topics.title: 3.1 Cell theory, cell types and organelles

sections.heading: Cell theory and cell organization
bullets: The classical cell theory states that organisms are made of cells, the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life, and new cells arise from pre-existing cells.
Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; their DNA occupies a nucleoid region. Bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes.
Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Plants, animals, fungi and protists are eukaryotes.
Cell size is limited in part by the relationship between surface area and volume: as a cell grows, volume increases faster than surface area, making exchange less efficient.

rows: Selective boundary controlling exchange and cell signaling
Stores most DNA and regulates gene expression
Makes and processes proteins for membranes or secretion
Lipid synthesis, detoxification and calcium storage
Modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids
Produces much of the cell's ATP during aerobic respiration
Digests and recycles materials in many animal cells
Carries out photosynthesis in plants and many algae
Storage and water balance; a large central vacuole supports plant cells
Provides support and protection in plants, fungi and many prokaryotes

sections.heading: Membrane transport
bullets: The fluid-mosaic membrane is a flexible phospholipid bilayer containing proteins and other molecules. Selective permeability means some substances cross more easily than others.
Simple diffusion moves particles down their concentration gradient without cellular energy. Osmosis is the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane.
Facilitated diffusion moves substances down a gradient through channel or carrier proteins; it does not directly use ATP.
Active transport moves substances against a gradient and requires energy, directly or indirectly. The sodium-potassium pump is a common example in animal cells.
Endocytosis brings materials into a cell in vesicles; exocytosis releases materials when vesicles fuse with the membrane.
A cell in a hypertonic solution tends to lose water; in a hypotonic solution it tends to gain water. Isotonic conditions produce no net water movement.

sections.heading: Exam review
bullets: State the three principles of cell theory and compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
Match major organelles to their functions and explain why plant and animal cells differ in some structures.
Compare diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport by direction, protein involvement and energy use.
Predict water movement when a cell is placed in a hypertonic or hypotonic solution.

units.title: Chapter 4 - Cellular Metabolism and Metabolic Disorders

sections.heading: Metabolism and enzymes
paragraphs: Metabolism is the complete set of chemical reactions in a cell or organism. Catabolic pathways break molecules down and release energy; anabolic pathways use energy to build complex molecules. ATP links energy-releasing processes to energy-requiring work.
bullets: Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually proteins, that lower activation energy. They increase reaction rate without changing the reaction's overall energy difference.
Enzyme activity depends on substrate availability, temperature, pH and regulatory molecules. Extreme temperature or pH may alter the active site's shape and reduce activity.
Pathways are regulated so that products do not accumulate unnecessarily. Feedback inhibition occurs when a pathway's end product inhibits an earlier enzyme.

sections.heading: Cellular respiration
paragraphs: Cellular respiration transfers energy from food molecules to ATP. In aerobic respiration, glucose is oxidized using oxygen and the products include carbon dioxide and water: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + usable energy (captured partly in ATP).
bullets: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and splits glucose into pyruvate, producing a small amount of ATP and reduced electron carriers.
When oxygen is available, pyruvate is processed and the citric acid cycle releases carbon dioxide and transfers high-energy electrons to carriers.

The electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane uses electron energy to establish a proton gradient. ATP synthase uses this gradient to make ATP; oxygen is the final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration.
Without oxygen, fermentation regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue, but it yields far less ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration.
Cellular respiration is not the same as breathing: breathing exchanges gases at the organism level, while respiration refers to cellular energy-releasing reactions.

sections.heading: Photosynthesis
paragraphs: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in organic molecules. In plants and many algae, chloroplasts capture light and use carbon dioxide and water to make carbohydrates, releasing oxygen as a by-product.
bullets: Light-dependent reactions occur in thylakoid membranes. They capture light energy, split water, release oxygen and produce ATP and NADPH.
The Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma and uses ATP and NADPH to incorporate carbon dioxide into carbohydrate precursors.

Photosynthesis and respiration are related but not reverse versions of every individual step. Photosynthesis stores energy in organic molecules; respiration transfers energy from those molecules to ATP.

sections.heading: Metabolic disorders and health
bullets: A metabolic disorder occurs when a biochemical pathway, enzyme, hormone or transport process does not function normally. Causes can include inherited variants, diet, infection or other environmental influences.
Diabetes mellitus involves problems with insulin production or response and disrupts regulation of blood glucose. Type 1 and type 2 diabetes have different main mechanisms and risk patterns.

A pathway explanation should identify the affected process, explain the change in normal regulation, and connect that change to effects on cells or the body. Avoid assuming every disorder has a single cause.

sections.heading: Exam review
bullets: Compare anabolism and catabolism and explain how ATP couples reactions.
Outline glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, noting locations and major outputs.
Compare aerobic respiration and fermentation by oxygen use, ATP yield and products.
Describe where light-dependent reactions and the Calvin cycle occur and what each produces or uses.

topics.title: 5.1 Inheritance, gene expression and evolutionary change

sections.heading: Genes, chromosomes and inheritance
paragraphs: Genetics studies heredity and variation. A gene is a segment of DNA that contributes to a functional product; genes are arranged on chromosomes. Different versions of a gene are alleles.
bullets: An organism's genotype is its genetic constitution for a trait; phenotype is its observable characteristic produced through genotype and environment.

In a simple dominant-recessive pattern, a dominant allele can determine phenotype in a heterozygote, while a recessive phenotype generally appears when both alleles are recessive. Many real traits do not follow this simple pattern.

Mendel used controlled crosses in pea plants to infer patterns of inheritance. His principles include segregation of allele pairs into gametes and independent assortment for genes that are inherited independently.
A Punnett square organizes possible allele combinations from parents. It predicts probabilities, not guaranteed outcomes for each child.
Sex-linked inheritance involves genes on sex chromosomes. In humans, many X-linked recessive traits appear more often in males because males generally have one X chromosome.

sections.heading: DNA replication, gene expression and mutation
bullets: DNA replication copies genetic information before cell division. Complementary base pairing allows each original strand to guide synthesis of a new strand; the result is semiconservative, with one old and one new strand in each DNA molecule.
In transcription, RNA polymerase uses a DNA template to make RNA. In translation, ribosomes read mRNA codons and tRNAs bring amino acids to build a polypeptide.
A codon is a three-base sequence in mRNA. The genetic code has start and stop signals and is redundant, meaning several codons may specify the same amino acid.

Mutations are changes in genetic material. They can be neutral, harmful or beneficial in a particular environment. Substitution, insertion and deletion may affect a protein; insertions or deletions can shift the reading frame.
Chromosomal changes can involve deletion, duplication, inversion or translocation of segments. Mutations provide new genetic variation, but their consequences depend on location and context.

sections.heading: Cell division and reproduction
bullets: The cell cycle includes growth and DNA replication followed by division. Mitosis produces two genetically similar daughter cells for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
Meiosis involves two divisions and reduces chromosome number to produce haploid cells. Crossing over and independent assortment create genetic variation.
Fertilization restores the diploid chromosome number by joining haploid gametes. Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from two parents.
Binary fission is a common form of cell division in prokaryotes. Asexual reproduction can produce genetically similar offspring, while sexual reproduction usually increases variation.

sections.heading: Evolution and natural selection
bullets: Evolution is change in inherited characteristics of populations across generations. Individuals do not evolve genetically during their own lifetime; populations change as allele frequencies shift.

Natural selection occurs when heritable differences affect survival or reproductive success in a particular environment. Individuals with advantageous traits tend to leave more offspring, so those traits may become more common.
Variation can arise through mutation and genetic recombination. Gene flow, genetic drift and mutation can also change allele frequencies; selection is not the only evolutionary mechanism.

Evidence for evolution includes fossils, comparative anatomy, embryology, biogeography and molecular similarities. Shared structures can indicate common ancestry, while analogous structures can result from similar selective pressures.
Adaptation is a population-level outcome across generations. Evolution has no predetermined goal and does not mean that organisms always become more complex.

sections.heading: Exam review
bullets: Use a simple genetic cross to calculate genotype and phenotype probabilities, stating assumptions.
Compare mitosis and meiosis by number of divisions, chromosome number and genetic similarity.
Trace information from DNA through RNA to protein and explain how a mutation might affect the product.
Explain natural selection using variation, heritability, differential reproductive success and change across generations.

sections.heading: Infectious agents and transmission
bullets: Pathogens are agents capable of causing disease. They include bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and some parasitic worms. Not every microorganism is harmful; many are harmless or beneficial.

Infection occurs when an agent enters a host, attaches or invades, multiplies and overcomes defenses sufficiently to cause damage. Transmission can occur through contact, contaminated food or water, droplets, vectors or other routes.

Infectious disease risk depends on the pathogen, route and dose of exposure, host defenses and environment. Prevention can interrupt transmission through sanitation, safe food and water, vaccination, ventilation and appropriate infection-control practices.
Antibiotics act against susceptible bacteria, not viruses. Using antibiotics only when appropriate and as prescribed helps reduce the spread of antimicrobial resistance.

sections.heading: Innate defenses
bullets: Innate immunity provides rapid, broad protection. Physical and chemical barriers include skin, mucous membranes, tears, stomach acid and antimicrobial secretions.
Inflammation recruits immune cells and molecules to affected tissue. Fever and inflammation are defensive responses, but severe or prolonged responses can also harm the body.
Phagocytes such as macrophages engulf microbes and debris. Natural killer cells can destroy some infected or abnormal cells. Complement proteins help mark or damage microbes and promote inflammation.
Innate defenses do not target one unique antigen with the same precision as adaptive immunity, but they help activate and guide adaptive responses.

sections.heading: Adaptive immunity
bullets: Adaptive immunity recognizes particular antigens and develops immunological memory. Its two major arms are humoral immunity and cell-mediated immunity.
B lymphocytes can become plasma cells that secrete antibodies. Antibodies bind specific antigens and can neutralize pathogens, mark them for destruction or activate complement.
Helper T cells coordinate immune responses by signaling other cells. Cytotoxic (killer) T cells can destroy infected cells displaying relevant antigen.
Memory B and T cells remain after an immune response and can make a later response faster and stronger.

Vaccination exposes the immune system to a safe form or component of an antigen so memory can develop without requiring the disease itself. Passive immunity provides ready-made antibodies and is temporary.

sections.heading: Immune disorders and HIV
bullets: Allergy is an excessive response to a usually harmless antigen. Autoimmunity occurs when immune responses target the body's own components; immunodeficiency means one or more defenses are impaired.

HIV infects cells including CD4 helper T cells. As immune function is weakened, the person becomes more vulnerable to opportunistic infections and some cancers; AIDS is the advanced stage of HIV infection as defined by clinical criteria.

HIV is transmitted through specific body fluids, not through ordinary casual contact such as sharing a classroom or handshake. Prevention and care rely on accurate testing, effective medical treatment and reducing exposure routes.
Immune tolerance helps prevent attacks on self. A failure of tolerance can contribute to autoimmune disease; an exaggerated response to external antigens can cause hypersensitivity.

sections.heading: Exam review
bullets: Distinguish pathogen, infection and infectious disease; name several transmission routes.
Compare innate and adaptive immunity by speed, specificity and memory.
Explain the roles of antibodies, B cells, helper T cells and cytotoxic T cells.
Compare vaccination and passive antibody protection and explain why antibiotics do not treat viral infections.

sections.heading: Why classify organisms?
paragraphs: Taxonomy is the science of naming, describing and classifying organisms. Classification organizes biodiversity, supports identification and helps scientists communicate relationships consistently.
bullets: Early systems often grouped organisms by visible similarities. Modern classification considers multiple forms of evidence, especially evolutionary relationships and molecular data.
A classification should reflect evidence about shared ancestry, but scientific systems can change when new evidence becomes available.

A taxon is a named group at any rank. A species is commonly treated as a group of populations whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring, though this definition does not fit every organism or fossil.

sections.heading: Taxonomic ranks and scientific names
bullets: A common hierarchy from broad to specific is domain, kingdom, phylum (division in some plant classifications), class, order, family, genus and species.

Binomial nomenclature gives each species a two-part Latinized name: genus followed by specific epithet, for example Homo sapiens. The genus begins with a capital; the epithet is lowercase; both are italicized when printed.

Scientific names reduce confusion caused by different common names across languages and regions. Names follow internationally coordinated codes, with separate conventions for different groups of organisms.

rows: Prokaryotic cells; immense diversity of metabolism and habitats
Prokaryotic cells with distinct molecular features; many live in ordinary as well as extreme environments
Cells with nuclei; includes animals, plants, fungi and diverse protists
Mostly multicellular photosynthetic eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls
Absorptive heterotrophs; cell walls commonly contain chitin
Multicellular heterotrophs that ingest food; cells lack walls
Diverse eukaryotes that do not fit neatly into plant, animal or fungal kingdoms

sections.heading: Evidence and identification
bullets: Organisms can be compared using cell structure, anatomy, development, physiology, behavior, fossils and DNA or protein sequences.
A dichotomous key identifies an organism through a sequence of paired contrasting choices. Correct identification depends on observing the stated features carefully.

Similar appearance does not always mean close relationship: convergent evolution can produce analogous traits in unrelated groups. Homologous traits are similar because of shared ancestry, even if their current functions differ.
Classification is a model of relationships based on available evidence, not a fixed list that can never be revised.

sections.heading: Exam review
bullets: Write taxonomic ranks in order and format a binomial scientific name correctly.
Compare bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes by cell organization.
Explain why modern classification uses molecular evidence alongside visible features.
Describe how a dichotomous key works and distinguish homologous from analogous structures.

units.title: Chapter 8 - Ecology and Conservation of Natural Resources

sections.heading: Ecological levels and interactions
bullets: Ecology studies relationships among organisms and between organisms and their environment. Levels include organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome and biosphere.
A habitat is where an organism lives; its niche describes its ecological role, resource use and interactions. Competition occurs when organisms use a limited shared resource.
Predation benefits the predator and harms prey; mutualism benefits both partners; commensalism benefits one without a major effect on the other; parasitism benefits one while harming its host.
Food chains show energy transfer along one pathway; food webs show interconnected feeding relationships. Producers capture energy, consumers obtain it by feeding, and decomposers recycle nutrients.
Energy flows through ecosystems and is lost as heat at each transfer. Matter, including carbon and nitrogen, cycles through organisms and the physical environment.

sections.heading: Ecosystems and biomes
bullets: Terrestrial biomes such as forests, grasslands, deserts and tundra are shaped by climate, especially temperature and precipitation, as well as soils and disturbance.
Freshwater ecosystems include rivers, streams, lakes, ponds and wetlands. Flow, depth, oxygen, nutrients and light shape the communities present.
Marine ecosystems include coastal zones, coral reefs, estuaries and open ocean. Salinity, depth, light and nutrient availability influence productivity and species distribution.
Biodiversity includes genetic diversity, species diversity and ecosystem diversity. It supports ecological processes and can increase resilience, although no ecosystem is immune to disturbance.

sections.heading: Pollution and human impacts
bullets: Pollution is the introduction of substances or energy that causes harmful environmental change. Major forms include air, water, soil, noise, thermal and radioactive pollution.
Water pollution can result from sewage, pathogens, agricultural runoff, industrial chemicals, plastics or sediment. Excess nutrients may cause eutrophication, algal growth and oxygen depletion.

Soil pollution can arise from pesticides, heavy metals, waste disposal and industrial activities. Air pollution includes particulate matter and harmful gases from transport, industry, burning and natural sources.
Deforestation, habitat fragmentation, overharvesting, invasive species and climate change can reduce populations and disrupt ecosystems. Effects often interact rather than acting alone.

sections.heading: Conservation and sustainable use
bullets: Conservation protects biodiversity and maintains natural resources for present and future needs. In-situ conservation protects species in their natural habitats; ex-situ conservation protects them outside those habitats, for example in seed banks or conservation centers.
Protected areas, habitat restoration, sustainable harvesting, pollution control and community stewardship can support conservation when adapted to local conditions.
The three pillars of sustainability are environmental protection, social well-being and economic viability. Good resource management considers trade-offs, fairness and long-term effects.
A useful case-study answer identifies the pressure, the affected ecosystem or resource, the evidence of impact, and a feasible action with a way to monitor success.

sections.heading: Exam review
bullets: Distinguish population, community and ecosystem using examples.
Explain energy flow through trophic levels and contrast it with nutrient cycling.
Compare freshwater and marine ecosystems or describe the features of a terrestrial biome.
Name sources and effects of water and soil pollution and propose practical prevention or restoration measures.
Compare in-situ and ex-situ conservation and explain how sustainability guides resource use.

units.title: Chapter 9 - Introduction to Botany and Zoology

topics.title: 9.1 Plant diversity and major animal groups

sections.heading: Botany and major plant groups
bullets: Botany is the study of plants and plant-like organisms. Major areas include plant structure, physiology, taxonomy, ecology, genetics and economic botany.
Algae are diverse photosynthetic organisms, mostly aquatic. They range from microscopic single cells to large seaweeds and are important producers in aquatic food webs.
Bryophytes such as mosses lack vascular tissue and reproduce by spores; they generally depend on moist conditions for fertilization.
Seedless vascular plants such as ferns have xylem and phloem and reproduce by spores. Vascular tissue transports water, minerals and sugars through the plant.
Gymnosperms produce exposed seeds, often in cones. Angiosperms are flowering plants whose seeds develop within an ovary that becomes fruit.
Plant transport relies on xylem, which conducts water and minerals mainly upward, and phloem, which distributes sugars from sources to sinks.

sections.heading: Invertebrate animals
bullets: Invertebrates lack a vertebral column and include many different body plans. They are not a single evolutionary branch but a broad descriptive grouping.
Sponges have porous bodies and filter-feed; cnidarians such as jellyfish and hydra have stinging cells and often show polyp or medusa forms.
Flatworms are generally flattened; roundworms have cylindrical unsegmented bodies; annelids are segmented worms. Some members of these groups are parasites and others are free-living.

Mollusks commonly have a muscular foot, visceral mass and mantle, though these structures vary. Arthropods have jointed appendages, segmented bodies and an exoskeleton; they include insects, arachnids, crustaceans and myriapods.
Echinoderms are marine animals with a water vascular system and adult radial symmetry. Their larvae are typically bilateral.
Insects have three pairs of legs and three main body regions. Some undergo incomplete metamorphosis; others undergo complete metamorphosis with egg, larva, pupa and adult stages.

sections.heading: Vertebrate animals
bullets: Vertebrates are chordates with a vertebral column. Major groups include fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, with diverse adaptations to aquatic and terrestrial life.
Many fishes use gills and fins; amphibians typically have a life cycle linked to water and permeable skin; reptiles have keratinized coverings and amniotic eggs adapted to land.
Birds have feathers, wings and beaks, and most maintain high internal body temperatures. Mammals have hair and mammary glands; most give birth to live young, though monotremes lay eggs.
Agnathans are jawless vertebrates; gnathostomes possess jaws. Jaws and paired appendages enabled new feeding and movement strategies in vertebrate evolution.

Classification uses combinations of body structure, development, physiology and evolutionary evidence. A trait should be compared carefully rather than treated as universal for every member of a group.

sections.heading: Exam review
bullets: Compare bryophytes, seedless vascular plants, gymnosperms and angiosperms by vascular tissue and reproduction.
Name defining features of arthropods, mollusks, annelids, cnidarians and echinoderms.
Compare complete and incomplete metamorphosis and list the stages of each.
Compare fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals using respiratory, reproductive or body-covering adaptations.

topics.title: 10.1 Biology in health, industry and the environment

sections.heading: Applied biology
paragraphs: Biological knowledge is applied to improve health, food production, industry and environmental management. Applications use evidence from fields such as microbiology, genetics, immunology, ecology and physiology.
bullets: Medicine uses biological understanding in diagnosis, prevention, treatment, vaccines, drug development, transplantation and public health.
Agriculture applies plant, animal and microbial biology to crop improvement, soil health, pest management, animal production and food preservation.

Biotechnology uses organisms, cells or biological molecules to develop useful products and processes. Biosensors combine a biological recognition element with a signal-producing system to detect substances.
Environmental engineering applies biological processes to waste treatment, pollution control, ecosystem restoration and resource management.

sections.heading: Medical and genetic technologies
bullets: Immunodiagnostic tests detect antigens or antibodies to help identify infection or other conditions. Results must be interpreted with test accuracy, timing and clinical context in mind.

Immunotherapy uses or modifies immune responses to help treat disease. Transplantation requires attention to tissue compatibility and immune rejection; matching and immunosuppressive treatment can reduce risk.
Gene therapy aims to treat or prevent disease by changing, replacing, silencing or adding genetic material in cells. Delivery, safety, effectiveness and ethical review are essential considerations.

Recombinant DNA methods combine genetic material using laboratory techniques. A medically useful protein can be produced by inserting its gene into suitable cells, growing those cells under controlled conditions and purifying the product.
Industrial insulin production commonly uses engineered microorganisms or cell systems to make human insulin or its components. The final product requires careful purification and quality control.

sections.heading: Biological processes in environmental and industrial work
bullets: Wastewater treatment combines physical separation with biological processes. Microorganisms break down organic matter; treatment stages and disinfection reduce contaminants before discharge or reuse.
Bioremediation uses organisms or biological products to transform or remove certain pollutants. It is most suitable when the pollutant, organism and environmental conditions are compatible.
Single-cell protein refers to protein-rich microbial biomass that may be used as food or feed after safety, nutritional, production and environmental requirements are addressed.

Biological applications should be evaluated for effectiveness, safety, cost, accessibility, environmental effects and ethical implications. A technology's promise does not remove the need for monitoring and responsible oversight.

sections.heading: Exam review
bullets: Give examples of biology in medicine, agriculture, biotechnology and environmental engineering.
Explain the basic principle of an immunodiagnostic test, immunotherapy or gene therapy.
Outline how engineered cells can produce a therapeutic protein and why purification and quality control matter.
Describe the main purpose of biological wastewater treatment and state factors that should be considered before applying a biotechnology.
